In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 dev success on both seeds, and no training signals were reported, so I can't yet tell whether learning failed or the agent learned but doesn't generalise. Its design is already reasonable: layers go in as 2D channels, a footprint-pooling head gives per-cell logits, and pooled features drive the DONE and value outputs. The likely weak points are these:
- **Recipe:** 4 PPO epochs use up the budget on only about 131k samples, and gamma 0.95 is short for a +1 reward that only arrives at the end of a 6–33 step episode.
- **Receptive field:** about 5×5 with no global context passed back to each cell, which limits reasoning about build order and overhangs across the whole 8×8 grid.

Following the suggested split for round 1:
- **(a)** recipe only: 2 epochs (about 1.85× the samples), gamma 0.97, lambda 0.95.
- **(b)** a deeper network with global context fed back to every cell, on the default recipe.
- **(c)** both together.

Because dev success may stay at 0, I'll rank candidates by training success.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on mean training success over the last 10% of training, so the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. These were: two PPO epochs with a longer horizon (229k steps), a deeper residual network with global context (82k steps), and the two combined. None of them used much time (51–70 s of the 900 s allowed), so compute is the only limit that binds. Two things look likely to be wrong. First, the starting network has to infer the brick's landing layer (the highest filled cell across the footprint) and match it against the 'missing' channel at that layer. To do that it must mix all layers in a 1×1 stem, which is a hard and indirect computation. Second, with about 257 actions, an entropy coefficient of 0.01 may keep the sampled policy too spread out to ever finish an exact build. This round tests a network that treats each height layer as a separate example with shared weights (each layer sees its neighbours below and above), and a one-epoch, low-entropy recipe with about 426k steps. The candidates form a 2×2-style design, so the network effect and the recipe effect can be told apart.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 for both training success and dev success. That holds across three networks (the starting net, a deeper net with global context, and the per-layer net) and across 1, 2 and 4 PPO epochs. Because every result is 0, these runs cannot rank the networks: the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. One factor no trial has varied is the number of gradient updates. The default recipe makes about 4,096 Adam steps, using minibatches of 128 samples. The recipes tried so far made even fewer: r2c2 had about 400k samples but minibatches of 256, so it made only about 1,600 steps. The budget counts samples, not optimiser steps. So the smallest legal minibatch (64 samples, with n_envs 64) gives about 6,600 steps at 1 epoch or about 8,200 at 4 epochs. This round tests that idea on the starting net with 1 epoch and with 4 epochs. A third candidate uses a narrower residual net with a 9×9 receptive field and global FiLM, at about the starting compute and with the 1-epoch recipe, so its effect can be separated from the recipe's.

### Round 4
After 9 trials, training success is 0.000 on both seeds of every one, so learning itself is failing, not generalisation. None of the changes moved it: 1 to 4 PPO epochs, 82k to 408k samples, batch sizes from 64 to 512, lr 5e-4 or 1e-3, entropy 0.003 to 0.01, deeper nets, FiLM global context, or per-layer nets. When every recipe fails the same way, a mismatch between the world and its description becomes likely. All our networks share one assumption: the action index lines up with conv cell positions (type, y, x). If the world indexes actions differently (for example x and y transposed, or a different order), every per-cell head would be biased towards the wrong cells. Heads that need a fixed layout would then fail no matter how they are trained. This last round tests that idea. All three candidates keep the r2c2 recipe so results can be attributed. The candidates are: the starting network plus a zero-initialised flat linear head; a conv trunk with only a flat head; and a plain MLP over the flattened observation and mask.
